title: Representing inputs as vectors
goals: Encode a record using a fixed feature order and units
Distinguish a vector dimension from the number of examples
Detect missing values and target leakage before computation

prerequisite.prompt: A parcel classifier uses width and height to predict a class. Why must its final class label stay outside the input features?
prerequisite.answer: The class is the target being predicted. Supplying that answer as an input leaks information that would not be available for a new prediction.

vocabulary: An ordered list of numerical components
One value at a specified position in a vector
The number of components in a vector
The recorded feature order, units and validity rules

blocks.text: A neural network receives numbers in a specified order. Before learning how it computes, we need to represent one example without losing the meaning of its fields. A vector is an ordered list: [4, 2] can mean width 4 cm and height 2 cm if that is the declared order. Reversing the two numbers describes a different rectangle under the same schema.

For this fictional parcel investigation, use [width in cm, height in cm]. Width and height must both be present and greater than zero. The vector has dimension 2 because it contains two components. Record IDs identify examples; they do not measure the parcel. The target class is stored separately.
There are three examples, each with two features. Stacking their vectors makes a table with three rows and two columns. Do not confuse the number of rows with the dimension of one input.

Read fields by name, convert to the declared units, validate, and only then write the vector. Parcel D has width 50 mm and height 30 mm. Because 10 mm equals 1 cm, its encoded vector is [5, 3]. Writing [50, 30] would preserve the numbers while changing the physical meaning by a factor of ten.

blocks.title: Optional Python check

blocks.text: This short function assumes each supplied value is a number in mm or None for missing. It is a classroom example, not a complete input validator. Trace the conversion before running it. The function represents data; it does not fit a model or predict a class.

lesson.title: Read the same record through three stages

blocks.title: An input vector keeps an agreed order
blocks.caption: Read each row left to right, then assemble the final ordered pair. The schema explains the numbers; the vector alone does not.

blocks.label: Parcel E has width 20 mm and height 70 mm. Encode it and explain why [7, 2] is not the same input under this schema.

lesson.title: Repair a representation before using it

blocks.text: A missing height is unknown, not zero. Under this schema zero is also invalid, so reject the incomplete record and request the measurement. A different project might use a documented training-fitted replacement plus a missingness flag; that would be a different schema that must be applied consistently.

A changed field order must also change every consumer that reads positions. A vector can have the expected length and still be wrong because its order, units or meaning changed. A class label appended as a third component causes target leakage even if the software accepts three values.

lesson.title: Recognise the limits of an encoding

blocks.text: Two parcels can share width and height yet differ in material or weight. Their vectors are identical in this representation, so a deterministic model receiving only these features cannot distinguish them. Adding a feature changes the schema and dimension; it does not automatically improve predictions. Keep data splits and evaluation discipline from Grade 8.

blocks.label: Two records both encode as [4, 2] but have different target classes. What can this representation reveal, and what can it not reveal?

blocks.text: Next week, we will multiply each component by a matching weight and add the results. The computation is meaningful only if the feature order stays fixed.

workbook.title: Encode the records
workbook.prompt: Write A, B and C as ordered pairs from the lesson. State the dimension of each and the shape of the stacked table.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: A [4, 2], B [2, 4], C [3, 3]. Each has dimension 2. The table has 3 rows and 2 columns.

workbook.title: Convert before encoding
workbook.prompt: A new record has width 60 mm and height 10 mm. Give its vector in the agreed cm schema, and name one error in [60, 10].
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The vector is [6, 1]. [60, 10] uses mm numbers where cm numbers are expected, scaling both measurements tenfold.

workbook.title: Handle missing information
workbook.prompt: Width is 4 cm and height is missing. A teammate writes [4, 0]. Explain why this is invalid and give the action required by this schema.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: Missing is not measured zero. Height must be present and positive; reject the record and request a valid measurement before encoding.

workbook.title: Apply a new schema independently
workbook.prompt: A new toy battery task uses [temperature in degrees C, voltage in V, age in days]. Record K has voltage 5, age 12, temperature 18. Record L has temperature 20, voltage 4, age 0. Encode both; state the vector dimension and table shape. Age zero is valid. The future failure label is also supplied in the data file: should it be appended?
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: K [18, 5, 12], L [20, 4, 0]. Dimension 3, table 2 rows by 3 columns. Age zero is a valid known value. Exclude the future failure target from inputs; it is not available at prediction time.

workbook.title: Explain a collision
workbook.prompt: Two parcels have the same width and height but different material and target class. Explain why adding more examples alone cannot let this deterministic two-feature model tell these two inputs apart.
workbook.answer: Teacher explanation: The two input vectors are identical, so the fixed deterministic computation returns the same output. Additional rows do not create a missing distinction in these two vectors; a relevant available feature or an explicit uncertainty policy may be needed.

teacher.background: Begin Grade 9 by connecting the Grade 8 feature table to an ordered numerical input. Students should name every component before calculating. Use two 45-minute sessions. Avoid treating a vector as a mysterious neural object: the learning target is a precise data contract, including order, units, missing values and the distinction between inputs and targets.
materials: Printed lesson and workbook; paper and pencil
Calculator and optional local Python 3 editor; no packages or AI accounts needed
Use the fictional examples supplied; prepare the fresh retry before class
sessions: Ask the prerequisite question. Retrieve the distinction between a feature and a target; require a prediction-time explanation.
Place A, B and C on paper. Students label horizontal width and vertical height, then write vectors with the schema above them.
Complete W1 and W2. Contrast three examples with two components per example. Model the mm-to-cm conversion explicitly.
Trace the Python function or its paper equivalent. Complete the guided E case and compare the swapped vector.
Retrieve the schema without looking. Ask how two correctly sized vectors can have different meanings.
Use W3 and the identical-input example. Discuss valid zero in another schema without changing the parcel rule.
Collect W4 independently before giving hints. Check field order, dimensions, valid age zero and the excluded future target.
Use W5 and the exit response. Give targeted feedback, then administer the fresh retry and retain both attempts.
teacher.guidedAnswer: Guided E: [2, 7]. The reversed [7, 2] means width 7 cm and height 2 cm, a different measurement pair. Exit: [4, 2] reveals only width and height under the schema. It cannot reveal the omitted distinction causing different labels; the same deterministic input receives the same output.
misconceptions: A and B use the same numbers but assign them to different features. Read each position by name.
Rows count examples; components count features of one example.
Whether zero is valid depends on the field. Missing means unknown, and is not interchangeable with a measured zero.
teacher.assessment: Assess W4 for named order, all values retained, dimension 3, two-row shape and exclusion of the future label. Fresh retry: schema [mass in g, length in cm]; two records (length 4, mass 12) and (mass 9, length 6) encode as [12, 4] and [9, 6], dimension 2, table 2 by 2. Ask why an absent mass must not become zero without a declared policy.
teacher.support: Provide empty boxes labelled with feature names and units. Accept a correct spoken explanation before written notation. Extension: propose two different real objects that share the same two-feature vector, then identify an additional measurable feature available before prediction.
teacher.next: Week 2 uses the ordered components in dot products. Revisit order and signed multiplication before introducing weights.
